name: Kandal Kootam
tagline: Beach clean-ups and mangrove planting on the Kannur coast, every second Sunday.
about:
Kandal Kootam means 'the mangrove gathering', and that is how we began. In 2021, eleven people from Kannur and Payyannur met on the banks of the Pazhayangadi river with a sack of mangrove propagules and no idea how to plant them. A retired fisherman showed us. More than nine thousand of those saplings are standing in the mud today, and many are taller than we are.

Every second Sunday we're on a beach: Payyambalam, Meenkunnu, Muzhappilangad, Ezhara. We clean, sort and weigh what we find, and every quarter we send the numbers to the panchayats and the fisheries office, because data is harder to ignore than photos. In the planting season, from June to September, Sundays move to the river banks.

We're students, fisherfolk, retired teachers, engineers working from home, and a lot of children who are better at spotting microplastics than any adult. You don't need experience or equipment. You need old clothes, a water bottle and a willingness to get your feet muddy.

We don't do photo-op clean-ups. Every bag is sorted, every kilo is recorded, and the recyclables go to a women-run collection unit that pays fair rates.

events.name: Planting Day: A Thousand Propagules on the Pazhayangadi River

venue.name: Pazhayangadi river bank, near the old ferry point

events.about:
Our biggest planting morning of the season. One thousand propagules from Ajith's nursery, a stretch of eroded river bank, low tide at 7:40, and a hundred and twenty pairs of hands. Kunhiraman, who first taught us to plant in 2021, showed every group how deep to push a propagule, how far apart to space them, and why you plant from the water side first.

We planted all one thousand before the tide came back in at eleven. Each group adopted a numbered patch and will come back in December to count how many survived. Last year's survival rate on this bank was 71 percent, and we'd like to beat it.
events.guidelines: Wear clothes you're happy to ruin; the mud is knee-deep in places. Bare feet or old sandals that strap on. Bring water, a hat and a change of clothes. Children under 12 must stay with an adult on the upper bank. Follow your group leader in and out of the water; the river bed drops suddenly in some spots.

speakers.bio: Has planted on this bank every season since 2021 and keeps a survival count for every patch in a school exercise book.

events.name: Payyambalam Beach Clean-up #58
events.about:
Our fifty-eighth Sunday on a Kannur beach, and the first after the monsoon washed up everything the rivers had been carrying since June. We split the beach into six zones, gave each group a team leader and a set of sorting sacks, and picked until the sun got serious.

Then came the part that makes us different: sorting and weighing. Plastics into five types, glass, footwear, fishing nets, cloth and 'other'. Neenu read the weights aloud as each sack hit the scale. The morning's total was 486 kilograms, and the single most common item was the multilayer snack packet, which no recycler will take.
events.guidelines: Wear closed shoes; there is broken glass. We provide gloves, sacks and water. Never pick up syringes or anything medical; call a team leader, who has a sharps box. Leave shells, crabs and anything alive where you found it. Photos are welcome, but the sorting comes first.

events.name: Microplastics Detectives: A Workshop for Kids and Parents
events.about:
A Saturday afternoon for children aged eight to fourteen and the adults who bring them. Every family scooped a cup of sand from the tideline at Meenkunnu, sieved it, floated it in salt water, and counted the tiny coloured pieces under the field station's microscopes. One family found 214 pieces in a single cup.

Dr. Anjana explained where the pieces come from (mostly larger plastics breaking down in the sun) and what they do to the fish we eat. Then the children designed posters for their school notice boards, and the best three are now printed and up in schools in Azhikode and Valapattanam.
events.guidelines: One adult per family must stay throughout. The fee covers the sieves, magnifiers and snacks, and is per family, not per person. Wear clothes that can get wet and sandy. Please don't take samples home; they go into the field station's records.

events.name: Meenkunnu Beach Clean-up #61
events.about:
Clean-up number sixty-one takes us to Meenkunnu, a long, quiet beach that gets far fewer visitors than Payyambalam and far more fishing net. Low tide is at 7:05, which gives us about two hours on the wide, flat sand before the water returns.

As always, we'll pick in zones, then sort and weigh everything. This time the fishing nets go to a new partner: a group of women in Azhikode who weave old nets into floor mats. Bring a friend; Meenkunnu is long and we'll need every pair of hands.
events.guidelines: Closed shoes, a hat and water. Gloves, sacks and snacks are provided. Never touch syringes or medical waste; call a team leader. Leave anything living where it is. Children are welcome with an adult. The nearest bus stop is Azhikode junction, about a kilometre away; we can arrange a lift from there if you message us.

speakers.bio: Grew up on this stretch of coast and knows which corners of Meenkunnu the nets wash into.

events.name: Mangrove Walk and Talk at Kunhimangalam
events.about:
A slow morning walk through one of the richest mangrove stretches in north Kerala, with two people who know it best. Sreedevi teacher will explain how mangroves hold the riverbank together, filter the water and shelter the fish that coastal families depend on. Haridas, who has logged 160 bird species here, will help you spot kingfishers, herons and, with luck, a white-bellied sea eagle.

This isn't a planting day. It's a chance to see what a healthy, mature mangrove forest looks like, and to understand what we're trying to grow back on the eroded banks further south.
events.guidelines: Group size is kept small to avoid disturbing the birds. Wear muted colours and quiet footwear, and keep phones on silent. Binoculars help; we have six pairs to share. Stay on the path, and please don't break branches or collect propagules.

speakers.name: Sreedevi Panoli
speakers.bio: Taught biology for thirty-two years and still treats every walk like a field trip with a test at the end, only kinder.

speakers.name: Haridas Mangad
speakers.bio: Has logged 160 bird species in the Kunhimangalam mangroves and can name a kingfisher by its call from a hundred metres.
